text: A five-person IT team can run on tribal knowledge — everyone roughly knows what everyone else is doing. That breaks down past a few dozen staff, multiple shifts, or more than one office, where each team starts inventing its own definition of urgent, its own escalation habits, and its own idea of who can approve a change.
A formal ITSM framework fixes that by giving every team the same vocabulary and the same baseline process for the same kind of work, so consistency doesn't depend on who happens to be on shift.

Documented process is also often a legal requirement. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires publicly traded companies to maintain auditable internal controls over systems affecting financial reporting — in practice, documented change management: who requested a change, who approved it, who tested it, who implemented it. Internationally, ISO/IEC 20000 is the formal, certifiable standard for a service management system. Neither kind of audit is possible without consistent, written process to check against.

Mean time to resolution — MTTR — is the average time between an incident being reported and service being restored. Reactive support has no structure for shortening it; every incident starts from zero. A formal incident process shortens MTTR with triage criteria, a known escalation path, and a knowledge base of how similar incidents were resolved before — no extra staff required.

Most IT organizations run commercial platforms like ServiceNow or Jira Service Management alongside outside managed service providers, all built around the same shared vocabulary for incidents, problems, and changes. Without a common framework, a new vendor has to be explained from scratch. With one, it plugs into existing definitions on day one.

Consistency, auditability, and faster resolution — none of it requires more headcount, just a shared framework everyone actually follows. Next up: how ITIL itself evolved to become that framework, from its earlier rigid process model to ITIL 4.
